title: Optimal discriminator and the JS divergence
goal:
Check Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 numerically on a discrete $x$. Write four functions; `p_data` and `p_g` are 1-D probability vectors of the same length, and all logs are natural.

- `optimal_discriminator(p_data, p_g)` returns $D^*_G(x) = p_{\text{data}}(x) / (p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x))$ (Equation 2). Where both probabilities are 0, return `0.5`.
- `value(p_data, p_g, D)` returns $V(G, D) = \sum_x p_{\text{data}}(x)\log D(x) + p_g(x)\log(1 - D(x))$ (Equations 1 and 3). Use the convention $0 \log 0 = 0$, so a point with $p = 0$ adds nothing even when $D$ is 0 or 1 there.
- `jsd(p, q)` returns the Jensen-Shannon divergence $\tfrac12 \mathrm{KL}(p \Vert m) + \tfrac12 \mathrm{KL}(q \Vert m)$ with $m = (p + q)/2$.
- `virtual_criterion(p_data, p_g)` returns $C(G) = V(G, D^*_G)$ (Equation 4).
hints: Compute `denom = p_data + p_g`, divide only where `denom > 0`, and fill the rest with 0.5. `np.divide` with `out=` and `where=` does this in one call.
For `value`, mask each term: `np.where(p > 0, p * np.log(...), 0.0)`. Put a safe number inside the log for the masked entries, or NumPy warns and returns `nan`.
`jsd` only needs a small `kl` helper that sums over the points where its first argument is positive. The mixture `m` is positive wherever `p` is.
Theorem 1 gives you a self-check: `virtual_criterion(p, q)` must equal `-np.log(4) + 2 * jsd(p, q)` (Equations 5 and 6).
